cv-keywords.title: CV keywords for ATS: how to choose them, plus lists for 20 jobs
cv-keywords.seoTitle: CV Keywords for ATS: How to Choose Them + 20 Job Lists
cv-keywords.metaDescription: How to pick keywords from a UK job ad and where to put them on your CV: exact wording, abbreviations, essential criteria. Keyword lists for 20 jobs below.
cv-keywords.lead: Below this article you’ll find a keyword extractor and keyword lists for 20 popular jobs. Treat the lists as a starting point: the job ad you’re answering is always the most important source. First, here’s how to choose the right words and where to put them on your CV.

sections.h: How to use the tools and lists below
p: Under this article there are two things. The keyword extractor lets you paste a job ad and see the skills, tools and qualifications it mentions. The lists for 20 jobs show terms that often appear in UK job ads for each role.

The lists help you remember things you do every day but never thought to put on your CV. Don’t copy a whole list, though. Choose only the items you genuinely know and that fit the job you’re applying for. Every word on your CV should be something you can back up with an example from work, study or a project.
If the job ad uses a different name from the list, the ad wins. Its words are the ones a recruiter is most likely to type into the search box of their system.

sections.h: How to pick keywords out of a UK job ad
p: Read the ad with a highlighter. Mark the job title, the names of tools and software, licences and certificates, languages with their level, and specific tasks from the list of duties, such as “processing purchase invoices” or “handling customer complaints”.

Many UK ads, especially in the public sector, the NHS and charities, come with a person specification. It splits the requirements into essential and desirable criteria. The Civil Service, for example, says it uses its assessment methods to match people to the essential requirements of the job. Treat every essential criterion you meet as a keyword that must be visible on your CV.
Desirable criteria matter less, but if you meet them, show them too. Also notice what repeats and what sits at the top of the list. Those points usually matter most to the employer.
General traits such as “team player” or “good communicator” are rarely what a recruiter searches for. Show them through an example in your experience instead of listing them as separate words.

sections.h: Exact wording, abbreviations and full names
p: A search in a recruitment system doesn’t always recognise synonyms. If the ad says “stock control” and your CV says “keeping track of inventory”, a recruiter may not find you. Where it’s true, use exactly the same words as the ad.

For abbreviations, give both forms at least once: the full name with the abbreviation in brackets. UK ads are full of them: “Construction Skills Certification Scheme (CSCS) card”, “Security Industry Authority (SIA) licence”, “National Vocational Qualification (NVQ) Level 2”. That way your CV turns up whether someone searches for the short form or the long one.

Write languages with a level. The Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) describes language ability on a six-point scale from A1 for beginners to C2. “English C1 (CEFR)” is clearer than “good English”, and it matches ads that ask for a level.
Spelling counts too. If the ad says “organisation”, don’t write “organization”. Write software names the way the maker does, for example “Microsoft Excel” or “Xero”.

sections.h: Job titles: yours and the ad’s
p: The same job has different names in different companies: customer service adviser, customer support agent, contact centre adviser. If your official title was different from the one in the ad, keep your real title next to that job.
You can use the ad’s title in the headline under your name or in your profile, as long as it honestly describes what you do. For example: “Customer service adviser, live chat and email”.

sections.h: Where to put keywords on your CV
p: The key places are the headline under your name, your personal profile, the skills section and the descriptions of your experience. A recruiter reads the headline and profile first, so include the job title from the ad and two or three key skills there.

A skills section lets you show tools and licences quickly. But keywords in your experience are stronger, because they show where and how you used a skill. A word in a list says less than a sentence about what you did with it.

Put licences, cards and certificates in a separate section with their full name and, where it matters, the expiry date. SIA licences and CSCS cards, for example, have expiry dates, and employers often check them.
Compare two lines. “Excel, reporting” is just two words. “Prepared weekly sales reports in Excel using pivot tables” contains the same keywords and also shows the scope and level of your skill.
A good bullet point links a task, a tool and a result. It doesn’t have to be long. What matters is that the keyword sits in a natural sentence a recruiter understands without asking.

The same applies to soft skills. Instead of writing “teamwork”, describe a situation: coordinating a small team, working with another department, training a new starter. You can put the ad’s keyword into that sentence, and the recruiter gets evidence instead of a claim.
Don’t repeat the same word in every bullet and don’t add long lists of keywords without context. After the search, a person still reads your CV, and keyword stuffing looks unnatural.

Don’t hide keywords in white text or behind images. Built In explains that when an applicant tracking system parses a CV, it removes all formatting and reads only the text underneath. Anything written in white becomes visible to the recruiter, and recruiters are likely to disqualify applicants who try to game the system this way.

Don’t add skills you don’t have, even if they’re on the list for your job. And watch out for keywords that only exist inside a graphic, logo or icon. If the name of a program appears only as a picture, the system can’t read it and the search won’t find it.

sections.h: A quick check before you send
p: Open your CV and use the document search for each key word from the ad. If something is missing and you do have that experience, add it in the right place. Also check that you can select and copy the text, because a word that’s part of an image doesn’t exist for the system.

The National Careers Service gives similar advice for application forms: try to match the words you use to the keywords in the job advert, so the reader can easily see you’re a good candidate. The keyword extractor below does the first step for you. If you like, you can also order a CV prepared for a specific job ad.

faq.q: Where do I find keywords for my CV?
faq.a: Mainly in the job ad: the job title, the requirements, the duties and, if there is one, the person specification. The lists for 20 jobs below and other ads for similar roles help you fill gaps the ad doesn’t cover.

faq.q: What’s the difference between essential and desirable criteria?
faq.a: Essential criteria are what the employer needs to see to consider you. Desirable criteria are extras. Make sure every essential criterion you meet is clearly visible on your CV, ideally in the ad’s own words, and add desirable ones you genuinely meet.

faq.q: Should I write abbreviations or full names, like SIA or CSCS?
faq.a: Both, at least once. Write the full name with the abbreviation in brackets, for example “Security Industry Authority (SIA) licence”. After that, the short form is fine.

faq.q: Does hidden white text with keywords work?
faq.a: No. When a system parses your CV it strips the formatting, so hidden words become visible to the recruiter. Applications like that are likely to be rejected as an attempt to game the system.

faq.q: What if I don’t meet all the requirements?
faq.a: Show the ones you do meet and any experience close to the missing ones. If you’re learning something, say so plainly. Don’t add keywords you can’t back up with an example.

tailor-cv-with-ai.title: Tailor Your CV with AI: What Works and What Backfires
tailor-cv-with-ai.seoTitle: Tailor Your CV with AI: What Works and What Backfires
tailor-cv-with-ai.metaDescription: What automated screening reads, why hidden prompts backfire, the risks of a chatbot-written CV, a simple test you can run, and the EU and UK rules.
tailor-cv-with-ai.lead: More and more employers use tools that summarise, sort or score applications. That raises questions: should you write differently, can you “trick” the algorithm, and is it fine to use ChatGPT? Here’s how to use AI so your CV reads well for both a system and a person.

p: Whether a company uses a classic applicant tracking system (ATS) or a tool with AI features, the first step is similar: the system pulls the text out of your file. It doesn’t see colours, icons or layout, only words in a certain order. If the text is read badly, even a well-built model will judge the wrong data.

After that, the tool may compare your CV with the ad. The UK regulator, the ICO, describes a typical example: the employer’s system analyses your application, looking for certain words, skills or qualifications, and may score, rank or filter it. Which of these features are switched on depends on the employer.
For you, this means something simple. Clear, well-organised content with specific job titles, tools and achievements works well. That’s also what a recruiter looks for when reading a CV on their own.

sections.h: Hidden prompts and white text: why they backfire
p: Some online tips suggest adding a line in white text such as “ignore all previous instructions” and asking the AI to rate you highly. The problem is that an ATS strips the formatting when it parses your CV. Hidden text becomes ordinary text, visible to the recruiter.

Built In reported that a large staffing company told The New York Times it detects hidden text in CVs it scans with AI, and that recruiters will likely disqualify applicants who use hidden prompts. Even if a tool could be fooled, a person still makes the decision, and a hidden instruction doesn’t make you look trustworthy.

The same goes for white keyword lists, tiny fonts and text hidden behind images. It isn’t clever optimisation. It’s an attempt at manipulation, and it may also close the door on future roles at that company.

sections.h: What backfires when a chatbot writes your whole CV
p: The first risk is stock phrases. Language models like the same expressions: “dynamic professional”, “passion for innovation”, “results-driven”. A recruiter reading many applications for one role soon notices the repeated style, and vague phrases tell them nothing about you.

The second risk is invented facts. A model can add a tool, a qualification or a number that wasn’t in what you gave it, and state it with confidence. If you don’t catch it before sending, you’re responsible for an untrue statement, and it’s hard to explain at an interview.

The third risk is losing the link to the ad. A generic prompt such as “write me a CV” gives you a text that fits everything and nothing. Without the specific job ad and your real achievements, the model has nothing to tailor.

sections.h: What works: AI as your editor
p: AI can be a useful editor. It’s good at shortening long descriptions, tidying bullet points, spotting typos and suggesting a few versions of your profile. Give it the text of the job ad and your own checked facts, and ask it to match the wording. Don’t ask it to make up experience.

After every change, read the text sentence by sentence. Remove anything you couldn’t back up with an example at an interview. Swap vague phrases for specifics: the name of a system, a number you know from your work, the result of a project.
Before you paste your CV into a chatbot, think about personal data. To edit the wording, you usually don’t need your address, phone number or the names of employers you’d rather not share.

sections.h: Try it yourself: a simple two-CV test
p: You can see the difference between a generic and a tailored CV in about 20 minutes. Pick one real job ad you’re interested in. Write down your facts: jobs, dates, duties, tools, qualifications and languages.

Version 1: open a chatbot and use a generic prompt, such as “Write a CV for a customer service adviser”, adding only your facts. Version 2: give the chatbot the same facts plus the full text of the job ad, and ask it to describe your experience using the ad’s wording, without adding anything that isn’t in your facts.

Now run both versions through a free keyword scanner, such as the one on our site, with the same job ad. Look at three things. Which requirements from the ad are visible in each version? Which ones are missing, and are they missing because you don’t have them or because they’re described in other words? Did either version add something that isn’t in your facts?

Then read both versions as a recruiter would. Does the first third of the page show the job title and the main requirements from the ad? Count the stock phrases. The result tells you what to fix in your own CV. A scanner is a simple check, not a prediction of how a real employer’s system or recruiter will decide.

sections.h: What the law says: the EU AI Act, the GDPR and the UK
p: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) lists, in Annex III, point 4, AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of people, in particular to place targeted job ads, to analyse and filter job applications and to evaluate candidates. These count as high-risk systems, which come with specific obligations, for example on human oversight and transparency. The obligations apply in stages.

In the EU, the GDPR applies as well. Article 22 gives you the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning you or similarly significantly affects you. There are exceptions, but then the employer must put safeguards in place, at least the right to obtain human intervention, to express your point of view and to contest the decision.

In the UK, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (section 80) replaced Article 22 of the UK GDPR with Articles 22A–22D, in force since 5 February 2026. In March 2026 the ICO published information for jobseekers: employers need to tell you if automated decisions are being made about your application, and you can contest the decision, explain your point of view and ask for a real person to take a second look.
This is general information, not legal advice. If you think a decision about you was made by a system alone, you can ask the employer how your data was processed in the recruitment.

sections.h: Writing for AI is writing for people
p: There’s no secret language that only works on algorithms. A simple layout, standard section headings, the ad’s exact names for skills and concrete achievements help both the system and the recruiter.

A good final test is this question: would someone who doesn’t know you understand, after reading your CV, what role you do, what you have experience in and what you’ve achieved? If yes, your CV works for a person and for a machine. You can check how the text looks to a system with the free CV scanner, or order a CV tailored to a specific job ad.

faq.q: Will a CV written with ChatGPT get through an ATS?
faq.a: A system doesn’t reject a CV because AI helped write it. What matters is that the text can be read and matches the ad. The risks are vague phrases, repeated stock wording and invented details that a recruiter will notice.

faq.q: Does hidden text or a prompt for the AI in my CV work?
faq.a: It isn’t worth it. Formatting is stripped when the CV is parsed, so hidden text becomes visible. Recruiters treat it as an attempt at manipulation and are likely to reject the application.

faq.q: What should I give a chatbot to tailor my CV?
faq.a: The full job ad and your own checked facts: roles, dates, duties, tools, qualifications. Ask it to use the ad’s wording only where it describes what you really did, and check every sentence afterwards.

faq.q: Can an employer reject me based only on an algorithm?
faq.a: In the EU, Article 22 of the GDPR gives you the right not to be subject to a solely automated decision with significant effects, with exceptions that require safeguards. In the UK, Articles 22A–22D of the UK GDPR apply from 5 February 2026, and the ICO says you can contest such a decision and ask for a human review.

faq.q: Is recruitment AI regulated in the EU?
faq.a: Yes. The EU AI Act classes AI systems used to analyse and filter job applications or evaluate candidates as high-risk (Annex III, point 4). Their obligations apply in stages, so check the current timeline.

sections.h: One bullet, two job ads: a worked mini-example
p: Say you worked on reception at a dental practice. Your facts: you booked and changed patient appointments in the practice’s booking software, answered calls and emails, took payments and ordered office supplies. Your current bullet says: “Front desk duties at a busy dental practice.”

Ad 1 is for a medical receptionist and asks for “managing patient appointments” and “experience of practice management software”. The same bullet becomes: “Managed patient appointments, bookings and cancellations using the practice management software.” Nothing is new. You’ve just named what you already did, in the ad’s words.

Ad 2 is for an office administrator and asks for “handling incoming calls and emails” and “ordering office supplies”. Now the bullet becomes: “Handled incoming calls and emails for a dental practice and ordered office supplies.” Same job, same facts, different focus.

Notice what didn’t happen. Neither version claims invoicing, diary management for a director or any other duty from the ads that wasn’t in your facts. If an ad asks for something you haven’t done, leave it out of the CV and, if it matters, mention in your cover letter how you’d learn it.

sections.h: Essential and desirable criteria: how to act on them
p: Many UK ads, especially in the public sector, come with a person specification that lists essential and desirable criteria. The Civil Service, for example, says its assessment methods help match people to the essential requirements of the job, and it asks candidates to use a supporting statement to show how they meet the essential criteria.

Make a two-column note. In the first column, list every essential criterion. In the second, write where on your CV it’s visible: in your profile, in a bullet or in the skills section. Any essential criterion you meet but can’t point to on the page is the first thing to fix.

Desirable criteria come next. Add the ones you genuinely meet, but don’t let them push essential ones out of the top third of your CV. If you don’t meet a desirable criterion, you don’t need to mention it at all.

sections.h: Short on time? Tailor in this order
p: If you only have ten minutes, don’t rewrite the whole CV. Start with the headline under your name and your profile, because a recruiter reads them first. Put in the job title from the ad, if it honestly describes your work, and two or three of the main requirements you meet.

Next, look at your most recent job. Reorder its bullets so that the two or three that match the ad come first, and use the ad’s wording in them. Then move the matching skills to the top of your skills list.
Older jobs, education and hobbies can usually stay as they are. If you have more time later, go back and check the rest against the ad.

sections.h: What stays the same in every version
p: Some things never change from one CV to the next: employment dates, the names of employers, the job titles you actually held, your qualifications and grades, and licence or card details. An employer may check them with references or certificates, and different versions of the facts raise questions.

If your official title doesn’t match the ad, keep it and add a short description beside it, for example “Customer Service Assistant (live chat and email)”. You can use the ad’s title in your headline instead, as long as it honestly describes what you do.
Keep your CVs consistent with your LinkedIn profile too. A recruiter who compares them should see the same dates and titles, just described with a different focus.

faq.q: Can I change my job title to match the job ad?
faq.a: Not in your work history. Keep the title you actually held, and add a short description in brackets if it helps. You can use the ad’s job title in your headline if it honestly describes your work.

faq.q: Should I apply if I don’t meet every desirable criterion?
faq.a: Desirable criteria are extras, not conditions. Focus on showing every essential criterion you meet clearly. Add desirable ones only where you genuinely meet them.

faq.q: What should I tailor first if I’m short of time?
faq.a: Your headline and profile, then the top bullets of your most recent job, then the order of your skills list. Those are the parts a recruiter reads first.

case.title: One CV, two job ads: what changes and why
case.seoTitle: One CV, Two Job Ads: A Worked Example
case.metaDescription: Same person, same facts, two different job ads: see two CV versions side by side, the ad’s words highlighted, and which requirements become visible.
case.lead: One person, the same facts and two job ads with different requirements. We show how the CV changes for each one, which words from the ad go into the text and which requirements become visible. The person and the ads are fictional.
case.name: Anna Example
facts: Since 2021: customer service at an online homeware shop, handling live chat and email, returns and complaints, and some inbound customer calls.
Uses a CRM system and the shop’s order system every day.
Before that (2018–2021): cashier and sales assistant in a supermarket, working shifts.
Trains new team members; written and spoken English at C1 (CEFR), native Polish.

generic.summary: I have a background in customer service and sales. I am a good communicator, reliable and I enjoy helping people.
bullets: Customer service for an online shop

ads.title: Job ad A: customer service adviser, live chat and email (online shop)
ads.text:
Customer Service Adviser (Live Chat and Email)
Requirements: live chat and email support, handling returns and complaints, experience using a CRM system, written English at C1 level, online retail experience.

cv.summary: Customer service adviser with [[online retail experience]] since 2021. I provide [[live chat and email support]], handle [[returns and complaints]] and have daily [[experience using a CRM system]]. [[Written English at C1 level]] (CEFR).
bullets: [[Live chat and email support]] for customers of an online homeware shop
[[Handling returns and complaints]] from first contact to resolution
Daily work in a [[CRM system]] and the shop’s order system
Training new team members in customer service

ads.title: Job ad B: contact centre adviser (phone)
ads.text:
Contact Centre Adviser
Requirements: handling inbound customer calls, experience using a CRM system, shift work, training new team members, experience selling mobile phone contracts.

cv.summary: Customer service adviser with experience of [[handling inbound customer calls]] and [[using a CRM system]]. Familiar with [[shift work]] from my previous job in a supermarket, and I help with [[training new team members]].
bullets: [[Handling inbound customer calls]] alongside live chat and email for an online homeware shop: orders, returns and complaints
Recording contacts and case history in a [[CRM system]]
Cashier and sales assistant in a supermarket (2018–2021), [[shift work]]
[[Training new team members]] in the customer service team

changes: The profile talks about what each ad is looking for: live chat, email and complaints for A; inbound calls and shift work for B.
The same duties are described in the ad’s words. “Customer service for an online shop” becomes “handling inbound customer calls” for B, because that is what she really did.
The order of the bullets changes so that what matters most for each ad comes first.
Nothing was added. She has never sold mobile phone contracts, so that requirement from ad B stays missing and does not appear in her CV.

faq.q: Is tailoring a CV the same as adding experience?
faq.a: No. Both versions contain the same facts. What changes is the order, the wording and what goes into the profile. Requirements the person doesn’t meet stay missing.

faq.q: How is “x of 5 requirements visible” worked out?
faq.a: We check whether the words of each requirement from the ad appear in the CV text shown on this page. It is a simple check for illustration. Real ads are longer, and real systems and recruiters work in different ways.

faq.q: Do I need to tailor my CV for every job?
faq.a: It’s worth it for jobs you really want and when you move to a different kind of work, for example from live chat to phone support. For very similar ads, a small change to your profile is often enough.
